newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UK banks give qualified welcome to new regulator.
newsitem.headline: UK banks give qualified welcome to new regulator.

text.p: British bankers on Thursday gave a qualified welcome to government plans to put bank regulation under an enlarged Securities and Investment Board (SIB) but one called for it to have a sharper strategic focus.
In an interview with Reuters at an industry seminar sponsored by NCR, George Mathewson, chief executive of Royal Bank of Scotland, said he hoped for a greater focus on industry developments.
"I want to see much more attention paid to the strategic evolution of the banking industry at the top levels of the regulatory bodies," he said.
"I don't believe that has been done up to now and we have to stop fighting yesterday's battles."
Mathewson gave the example of the collapse of blue-blooded British merchant bank Barings in 1995.
"It could be said they were doing business that they should not have been doing and were enjoying a credit rating miles ahead of what they should have had."
He said the regulator (the Bank of England) should have been encouraging Barings to get out of the business it was in or to merge with a larger, more heavily capitalised partner.
Barings collapsed in February 1995 after Singapore-based trader Nick Leeson ran up losses of 800 million pounds ($1.3 billion) in unauthorised derivatives trades.

It was rescued by Dutch financial giant ING which has transformed it into its own investment banking arm ING Barings. The Bank of England, criticised for its handling of the affair, later revamped its supervisory structure.
Mathewson also mentioned last year's scandal at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) which would have had problems surviving if it had not been owned by a larger parent -- Deutsche Bank.
MGAM lost millions of pounds as a result of irregularities in three of its funds.
Mathewson said there appeared to be opposition to making regulation, especially of retail banking, cheaper by rationalisation.
Earlier this month, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown announced that regulation of the British banking industry would pass from the central bank to an enlarged SIB.
Mathewson's comments on costs were echoed by Peter Birch, chief executive of Abbey National, who said the price of regulation was "astronomical".
"It's the biggest growth indusry in Britain," he said.
"Politicians will support it because they say it protects the customer and it does, but they never say it's the customer who pays for it."
Birch said cases like Barings and the BCCI fraud happen infrequently and will happen whoever regulates the industry.
He welcomed the government's plan for an enlarged SIB but Mathewson was more circumspect, saying that the detailed proposals would have to be seen before a real judgement could be made.
The Abbey National chief was more upbeat.

"What I welcome more than anything else is that this new government has given priority to regulatory issues," Birch said, adding that banks, insurers and building societies were converging all the time and that one authority is essential.
He also laid emphasis on consistency.
"Up to now, we have had a lot of regulators falling over one another, now there will be one boss who will apply the same set of rules to everyone."
Birch also said he was waiting for a detailed bill which should be published in the next year or so and hoped that it would not produce an overlarge bureaucracy.
He said it was absolutely essential the new regulator was also given responsibility for the remaining building societies who will still have 17 percent of the British mortgage market.
"Building societies offer pretty well the same services as banks so they need to be included," he said.
